title: Accessing Grants, Loans & Partnerships
subtitle: Choose the right kind of growth money for one real business need, prove you are ready, and secure it without putting your business at risk.
description: An advanced, hands-on course for women who already run a working business and want funding to grow. You will match a costed need to a grant, loan or partnership, check your readiness, avoid scams, do the loan arithmetic yourself, negotiate partnerships, and finish with a Funding Readiness Pack and a 90-day plan.
outcomes: Write a costed, specific funding need and choose the right route: own money, grant, loan or partnership
Score your readiness on six areas and close the most important gaps
Verify lenders and programmes and recognise grant and loan scams
Calculate the true cost of a loan, compare flat and reducing-balance quotes, and test repayment against your worst month
Design a partnership deal, calculate its cash gap, and list the terms of a written agreement
Assemble a Funding Readiness Pack and a dated 90-day plan for a named opportunity
audience: Women running an established small business in Nigeria or elsewhere in Africa who want funding, equipment or market access to grow.
tools: Smartphone with WhatsApp and a scanner or Google Drive app
Google Sheets or a notebook and calculator
Your business records and bank statements for the last six to twelve months
Your ID, BVN and CAC documents if registered

modules.title: Choosing the Right Funding and Getting Ready
modules.overview: Decide exactly what you need money for, which type of funding fits it, and how ready your business is to be trusted with it. You finish the module with a costed need statement, an honest readiness score and a shortlist of three verified opportunities.

lessons.title: Grant, loan, partnership or your own money: matching funding to the need
objectives: Name the four main sources of growth money and what each one costs you
Describe one business need precisely: what, how much, and what it will produce
Match a need to the funding type that suits it, using a simple decision flow
Explain why a loan should only fund things that bring money back in time to repay

blocks.text: Most women who come to this course already run a working business: a tailoring shop, a bakery, a farm, a provisions store, a soap or snacks line. Sales cover the daily costs, but a bigger step needs a lump of money the business cannot save quickly enough. A second industrial machine. A deep freezer. Materials for a large school order. A small shop instead of a table. This course is about getting that money, or the resources it would buy, **without putting your business or your home at risk**.
There are four places growth money can come from. Each has a different price. Not all prices are paid in naira.

blocks.name: finance
blocks.alt: A woman reviewing figures and money on a screen
blocks.caption: Before you apply anywhere, decide which kind of money suits the need you have.

head: Source
What it is
What it costs you
Best for
rows: Your own money (retained profit, savings, ajo or esusu payout)
Nothing to repay, but it is gone if the plan fails, and it may be your safety buffer
Small, low-risk steps and testing an idea
Money given for a purpose, usually by a foundation, NGO, government programme or company
No repayment, but heavy competition, long waits, strict rules on spending and reporting
Things with clear social or training value, equipment, first certification costs
Money borrowed and repaid with interest and fees on a fixed schedule
Interest, fees, and the risk of losing collateral or your credit record if you miss payments
Anything that brings money back fast enough to repay: stock, a machine that raises output
Another business or organisation contributes something you need: credit, equipment, space, buyers, training
Some control, a share of profit, or obligations you must keep
Market access, supplies on credit, shared equipment, bulk buying

blocks.text: Start with the need, not the money

The most common mistake is to look for "funding" first and decide what to do with it later. Funders and lenders spot this at once. Start instead with one **specific need** that you can describe in a single sentence: what you will buy or do, what it costs, and what result it will produce in numbers.

items: Weak: "I need money to grow my fashion business."

Strong: "I need one industrial straight-stitch machine and one overlock machine, about ₦650,000 (approximate) together, so I can sew 40 school uniforms a week instead of 15 and accept the two school contracts I turned down last term."

blocks.text: The strong version tells anyone reading it what the money buys, why, and how it will pay for itself. It also tells **you** which type of funding fits. A machine that lets you accept paid orders you are already being offered can be repaid from those orders, so a loan or a supplier partnership is reasonable. A training programme for ten unemployed young women in your area does not repay itself directly, so a grant is the natural fit.

blocks.title: Choosing the right funding route
items: Describe the exact need
Cost it in naira
Will it earn money back?
When, and how much?
Pick grant, loan or partner
blocks.caption: If the need earns money back quickly and reliably, borrowing can work; if it does not, look to grants, partners or your own savings.

blocks.text: Three questions that decide the route

items: **Will this need bring money back?** New stock, a machine for orders you already have, or packaging that lets you enter a supermarket usually will. A website redesign or a fancy signboard may not, at least not in a way you can measure.

**How soon, and how much?** Write the extra profit per month that the need will produce, and how many months until it starts. A loan repayment usually starts within a month of disbursement, so a slow return is a danger sign for borrowing.

**Can someone else supply the thing instead of the money?** A supplier who gives you 30 days to pay, a buyer who pays a deposit upfront, or a cooperative that shares a machine can remove the need for cash entirely.

blocks.title: Worked example: one need, three possible routes
blocks.context: For example, Hauwa runs a tailoring shop in Kaduna. A secondary school has offered her an order for 300 uniforms at ₦9,000 each (approximate), paid in two halves: 50% on order and 50% on delivery. Fabric and trims cost about ₦4,200 per uniform. She needs a second machine, about ₦350,000 (approximate), to deliver in eight weeks.
steps: The 50% deposit is ₦1,350,000. That covers all the materials (₦1,260,000) with ₦90,000 left over.
The machine is the real gap: ₦350,000 minus the ₦90,000 left from the deposit = ₦260,000 still needed.
Route A, own money: she has ₦150,000 saved, but it is her only buffer. Using all of it leaves no safety.
Route B, partnership: she asks the machine dealer about paying in instalments over three months. The dealer agrees to ₦120,000 down and ₦80,000 a month for three months, a total of ₦360,000.
Route C, loan: a microfinance bank quotes a loan that would cost more in interest and fees than the dealer's ₦10,000 extra, and takes two to three weeks to approve.
blocks.result: Hauwa pays the dealer's ₦120,000 deposit from savings, keeps ₦30,000 as a buffer, and pays the three instalments from the delivery payment and her normal monthly sales. She needed a partner, not a lender, and no grant fits a commercial order at all.

blocks.title: Never borrow to cover losses
blocks.text: If the business is losing money every month, a loan does not fix it. It adds a repayment to a business that already cannot pay its costs. First find out why you are losing money (prices too low, waste, credit sales not collected), fix that, and only then consider growth funding.
What each funder wants to see

Each type of funder asks a different main question. A **grant maker** asks: does this create the change we exist to support, and will this person spend the money honestly and report on it? A **lender** asks: will this business repay on time, and if it does not, how do we recover our money? A **partner** asks: what do we gain, and can she deliver her side reliably? You will prepare all three answers in this course, but you should know which question you are answering before you write a single word.

blocks.title: Funding is not only money
blocks.text: Many of the most useful deals for small producers are not cash at all: a distributor who collects from your shop, a church or school that gives you a market, a larger maker who lets you use their NAFDAC-compliant production space at agreed hours. Keep these in mind whenever you think "I need money".

takeaways: Start with one specific, costed need, never with "funding" in general.
Loans suit needs that earn money back quickly; grants suit needs with social value that do not repay directly.
A supplier, buyer or partner can sometimes provide the thing you need instead of cash.
Never borrow to cover ongoing losses.

activity.title: Write your funding need statement
steps: Choose one real growth need in your business right now.
Write it in one sentence: what you will buy or do, the approximate cost in naira, and the result in numbers (more units, more orders, new buyer).
Answer the three route questions: does it earn money back, how soon and how much, and could someone supply it instead of cash.
Write which route (own money, grant, loan or partnership) fits best, and one sentence explaining why.
Keep this statement: you will build on it in every lesson.
activity.evidence: A written need statement with cost, expected result and chosen route, photographed or saved in your notes.

lessons.title: The readiness check: what funders and lenders look at first
objectives: List the documents and records most Nigerian lenders and grant programmes ask for
Score your business honestly on six readiness areas
Explain why cash flow, not just profit, decides whether a loan can be repaid
Identify the two or three gaps to close before you apply

blocks.text: Funders cannot visit every applicant or follow her for a month. They judge you from **evidence on paper and on your phone**. The businesses that win are rarely the ones with the most moving story. They are the ones whose documents, records and track record agree with each other and with what they say in the application.

This lesson gives you a readiness check you can run in an evening. Be honest. A low score today is not a failure; it is a list of jobs to do before you waste time on an application you cannot yet win.

blocks.name: personal-documents
blocks.alt: A person sorting personal and business documents
blocks.caption: Funders judge you mostly from what you can show them: documents, records and history.

blocks.text: The six readiness areas

head: Area
What is usually asked for
Why it matters to them
rows: Valid ID (NIN slip, international passport, voter's card or driver's licence), BVN, CAC certificate for a business name or company
They must know exactly who they are dealing with; many grant programmes accept only registered businesses
An account in the business name, with 6 to 12 months of statements
Statements are independent proof of how much money really passes through the business
Sales, expenses, stock and debtors records; a simple monthly profit and loss
They show whether the business makes money and how steady it is
How long you have traded, past customers, any past loan repaid, references
Past behaviour is their best guide to future behaviour
Your costed need statement and how it produces results
They want to see money turning into a measurable result
Tax ID (TIN), and where relevant NAFDAC, SON or local permits
Some programmes and all serious partners will not deal with a non-compliant business

blocks.text: Your **BVN** links all your bank accounts to you, and banks and many lenders also check your credit history with licensed credit bureaus in Nigeria such as CRC Credit Bureau, FirstCentral and CreditRegistry. A missed loan repayment from an app two years ago can appear there. If you are unsure of your record, ask a bureau for your own credit report before you apply, so nothing surprises you.

blocks.title: Funding readiness check
items: ID, BVN and CAC ready
Business account with statements
Six months of records
Proof you deliver reliably
Costed plan for the money
TIN and product permits
blocks.caption: Score each line 0 (missing), 1 (partly there) or 2 (complete and up to date); 9 or less out of 12 means fix gaps before applying.

blocks.text: Profit is not the same as cash

A business can show a profit and still fail to pay a loan. That happens when money is tied up in stock or in customers who have not paid yet. Lenders are repaid from **cash in the account on the repayment date**, so they look closely at the pattern in your bank statements: steady inflows, or big gaps?

blocks.title: Worked example: Funmi's readiness score
blocks.context: For example, Funmi bakes bread and meat pies in Abeokuta and wants about ₦600,000 (approximate) for a bigger oven. She runs the six-area check.
steps: ID and registration: NIN and BVN yes, but no CAC certificate. Score 1.
Bank account: all sales go into her personal account mixed with family money. Score 0.
Records: she has a notebook of daily sales for eight months but no expenses. Score 1.
Track record: four years of trading, two schools buy weekly and would give references. Score 2.
Plan: she knows the oven cost and that it doubles her baking per batch, but has not worked out extra profit per month. Score 1.
Tax and compliance: no TIN; her packaged pies carry no NAFDAC number. Score 0. Total: 5 out of 12.
blocks.result: Funmi is not ready to apply yet. Her three priority gaps: register a business name with CAC and open a business account, start recording expenses so she can show monthly profit, and calculate the extra profit the oven would bring. She sets a 90-day target to raise her score to at least 10.

blocks.title: Three months of clean history beats none
blocks.text: If your sales currently go into a personal account, open a business account now and route every business payment through it, including POS and transfer sales. After three to six months you will have statements that speak for you. Funders often ask for six months or more, so the earlier you start, the sooner you qualify.
Choose your gaps wisely

You will probably find more gaps than you can close at once. Fix them in this order: first anything that makes you **ineligible** (no registration when the programme requires it), then anything that makes your numbers **unbelievable** (no records or bank history), and last anything that is simply nice to have. Two well-closed gaps are worth more than six half-started ones.

takeaways: Funders judge you from evidence: ID, BVN, CAC, bank statements, records and track record.
Business bank statements are your strongest independent proof; start routing all sales through one account now.
Lenders are repaid from cash on the due date, not from profit on paper.
Score yourself on six areas and fix eligibility gaps first.

activity.title: Run your own readiness check
steps: Copy the six readiness areas into your notebook or a phone note.
Score each one 0, 1 or 2, and write one line of evidence for the score (for example, "8 months of sales notebook, no expenses").
Add up your total out of 12.
Circle the two or three gaps that matter most, starting with eligibility.
Write one action and a date for each circled gap.
activity.evidence: Your scored readiness sheet with total, circled gaps and dated actions.

lessons.title: Where funding comes from in Nigeria, and how to spot fake offers
objectives: Name the main types of lenders, grant makers and partners open to small Nigerian businesses
Explain how to check that a lender or programme is real and licensed
Recognise the warning signs of grant and loan scams
Build a shortlist of three real opportunities that fit your need

blocks.text: Once you know your need and your readiness, the next question is where to look. Nigeria has many sources of growth money and partnership, but also many people pretending to be one. This lesson covers both: who is real, and how to tell.

blocks.name: bank
blocks.caption: Every lender you deal with should be licensed and checkable, whether it is a bank, a microfinance bank or a digital lender.

blocks.text: Lenders

head: Type
Examples of what they offer
Points to know
rows: Usually need a longer trading history, statements and sometimes collateral or guarantors
Small business and group loans, often weekly or monthly repayment
Licensed by the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN); closer to small traders, but rates are often higher
The Bank of Industry (BOI) lends to small, medium and larger enterprises and lists programmes for women-owned businesses on its website
Applications take longer and need stronger documents and a clear business plan
Member loans, ajo and esusu contributions
Often the cheapest and most flexible; you usually must save with the group first
Fast small loans on your phone
Very expensive for business use; only use lenders registered with the FCCPC, and read every charge

blocks.text: Grants and support programmes

Grant money for small businesses in Nigeria usually comes through **programmes**, not open gifts. Examples include foundations such as the Tony Elumelu Foundation entrepreneurship programme, government agencies such as SMEDAN (the Small and Medium Enterprises Development Agency of Nigeria), state government empowerment schemes, international development projects, and corporate social responsibility programmes run by banks and large companies. Many include training, mentoring or equipment rather than only cash, and almost all open for a short window each year.

Because programmes change every year, never rely on a list someone forwarded on WhatsApp. Go to the organisation's **official website or verified social media page**, read the current call, and note the opening and closing dates yourself.
Partners

items: **Suppliers** who sell to you on credit or instalments.
**Buyers and distributors** who pay deposits, give purchase orders, or carry your product to new markets.
**Larger businesses** that share equipment, space or certification, or buy from small producers as part of their supply chain.
**Associations and NGOs** that pool members for bulk buying, training or group loans.

blocks.title: Speed and cost of common sources
items: Thrift group: fast, low cost
Loan app: fast, high cost
Grant: slow, no repayment
Bank or BOI: slower, moderate cost
blocks.caption: Fast money is usually expensive money, and cheap money usually takes time to prepare for.

blocks.text: How to check that an offer is real

items: Find the organisation's official website yourself (do not click a link in a message) and confirm the programme is listed there.
For a bank or microfinance bank, check that it appears on the CBN's list of licensed institutions. For a loan app, check the FCCPC's published list of registered digital lenders.
Search the exact programme name plus the word "scam" or "fake" and read what comes up.
Ask: who is paying, and why? A real grant has a funder with a stated purpose and selection rules.
Never send money, your BVN, card details, OTP or PIN to anyone who contacts you about a grant.

blocks.title: The fee-before-grant trick
blocks.text: The most common scam goes like this: a message says you have been selected for a grant or a low-interest loan, but you must first pay a "processing", "registration", "insurance" or "release" fee. Real grant programmes do not ask winners to pay to receive their grant. Once you pay, the person disappears or asks for another fee. Delete the message, warn your group, and report it.

blocks.title: Worked example: Ifeoma checks two offers
blocks.context: For example, Ifeoma runs a small poultry farm near Owerri and needs feed and a few hundred day-old chicks before the festive season. In one week she receives two offers.
steps: Offer 1: a WhatsApp broadcast says a "Federal Women Empowerment Grant" of ₦500,000 is open; she must pay ₦15,000 to a personal account to "activate" her slot.
She searches for the programme on the relevant ministry's official website and finds nothing. The payment goes to an individual, not an organisation. She deletes it.
Offer 2: her microfinance bank offers a 4-month poultry loan. She checks the bank on the CBN list of licensed microfinance banks and finds it there.
She asks for the full repayment schedule in writing, including every fee, before agreeing to anything.
blocks.result: Ifeoma avoids losing ₦15,000 to a scam and moves forward with a licensed lender whose terms she can check. In Module 2 you will learn to test whether a loan like hers can actually be repaid.

blocks.text: Build your shortlist

Aim for a shortlist of three real opportunities that match your need and your readiness score. For each one, record: the name, the official link, what it offers, who is eligible, the deadline or how long approval takes, and the main documents required. Three well-chosen options are better than twenty you never complete.

takeaways: Lenders range from thrift groups and MFBs to commercial banks, BOI and loan apps, each with different speed and cost.
Grants come through time-limited programmes; always read the current call on the official site.
Check banks and MFBs against the CBN list and loan apps against the FCCPC list.
Never pay a fee to receive a grant, and never share your BVN, OTP or PIN.

activity.title: Build a three-opportunity shortlist
steps: Using your need statement from Lesson 1, list every possible source you know of: lenders, programmes, suppliers, buyers, groups.
Check each one on its official website or the relevant licensing list, and cross out any you cannot verify.
Pick the three best matches for your need and readiness score.
For each, record the name, official link, what it offers, eligibility, deadline or approval time, and documents required.
activity.evidence: A shortlist table of three verified opportunities with links and key requirements.

quiz.q: Bisi's provisions shop makes a small loss every month. She wants a ₦300,000 loan to "get back on her feet". What is the best advice?
options: Take the loan quickly before interest rates rise
Find and fix the cause of the monthly loss before considering any loan
Take a bigger loan so there is more cushion
Apply for a grant instead, since grants never need a plan
quiz.explain: A loan adds a repayment to a business that is already losing money. Fix the cause of the loss (pricing, waste, unpaid credit) first.

quiz.q: Which need is the strongest fit for a loan?
options: A community training day with no paid participants
Stock for confirmed orders that will be paid within six weeks
A new signboard to "look more professional"
Paying school fees
quiz.explain: Confirmed paid orders bring money back quickly and predictably, which is what a loan repayment needs.

quiz.q: Funmi scores 5 out of 12 on the readiness check. Her biggest gaps are no CAC registration and no business bank account. What should she do first?
options: Apply to every programme anyway
Register her business name and route all sales through a business account
Buy the oven on credit and explain later
Write a longer life story in her application
quiz.explain: Eligibility and evidence gaps come first. Registration and a clean business account make her eligible and believable.

quiz.q: A message says Ngozi has won a ₦1,000,000 grant but must pay ₦20,000 to release it. What is this most likely to be?
options: A normal grant step
A tax deduction
A fee-before-grant scam
An insurance requirement from the CBN
quiz.explain: Real grant programmes do not ask winners to pay to receive their grant. Asking for a release fee is a classic scam.

quiz.q: Why do lenders study bank statements so closely?
options: To see your personal spending habits for marketing
Because statements show the real cash flowing in and whether it is steady enough to meet repayments
Because banks are required to read every transaction aloud
They do not; only CAC documents matter
quiz.explain: Loans are repaid from cash on a due date. Statements are independent evidence of cash flow.

quiz.q: Hauwa needs a machine to fulfil a paid school order. The dealer offers instalments over three months for ₦10,000 more than the cash price. What kind of funding is this?
options: A grant
A partnership arrangement with a supplier
A digital loan
Equity investment
quiz.explain: The supplier provides the machine and lets her pay over time. That is supplier credit, a form of partnership.

modules.title: Applications, Accuracy and Loan Numbers
modules.overview: Turn applying into a repeatable process, check every figure before a reviewer does, and do the loan arithmetic yourself. You finish with a working tracker, a named document pack, a three-way number check and a tested loan decision.

lessons.title: Your application workflow: tracker, document pack and timeline
objectives: Break any funding application into clear stages with owners and dates
Set up a tracker that shows every opportunity and its next action
Build a reusable digital document pack with sensible file names
Plan backwards from a deadline so nothing is rushed

blocks.text: Applications fail for boring reasons far more often than for big ones: a missing document, a scanned certificate nobody can read, a form submitted an hour after the portal closed, a reference who never replied. The fix is to treat funding like any other business process, with a written workflow, a tracker and a ready pack of documents. In business language this is a **standard operating procedure (SOP)**: the same steps, done the same way, every time.

blocks.name: checklist
blocks.alt: A person ticking items on a large checklist
blocks.caption: A written workflow turns a stressful application into a list of small, finishable jobs.

blocks.text: The six stages of almost every application

items: **Confirm fit.** Read the full call or loan terms. Check eligibility line by line: location, sector, years trading, registration type, gender or age focus. If you fail any hard rule, stop.
**List requirements.** Copy every required document and question into your tracker. Note word limits and file size limits.
**Gather evidence.** Pull documents from your pack, request bank statements, ask referees early.
**Draft.** Write answers or fill the loan form using your need statement and numbers.
**Check.** Run the accuracy checks from Lesson 2 of this module. Ask one trusted person to read it.
**Submit and follow up.** Submit at least two days before the deadline, save the confirmation, and diary a follow-up date.

blocks.text: For a grant, Stage 4 is the biggest job, and the Institute's Proposal Writing course teaches each section in depth. For a loan, Stage 3 is usually the biggest, because lenders want statements, guarantor forms and sometimes a visit to your premises. For a partnership, Stages 1 and 4 become a conversation and a written agreement, covered in Module 3.
The tracker
Keep one tracker for all your opportunities. A Google Sheet on your phone works well, and so does a page in a notebook. The columns below are enough.

head: Opportunity
Type
Amount or offer
Deadline
Stage
Next action
By when
rows: Up to the amount on the call

blocks.text: Your document pack

Make one folder on your phone or Google Drive called **Funding Pack**, and inside it keep clear scans or photos (good light, flat, all four corners visible) of each document. Name each file so anyone can understand it: **2026-CAC-BN-Certificate.pdf**, **2026-03to08-Bank-Statement.pdf**, **NIN-Slip-Amina.jpg**. A free scanner app or the scan feature in Google Drive turns phone photos into tidy PDFs.

items: Identity: NIN slip or ID card, passport photograph
Registration: CAC certificate and status report if a company, TIN
Money: last 6 to 12 months of business bank statements, monthly profit and loss summary
Evidence: photos of products and workspace, customer letters or messages (with permission), past receipts for big orders
Plan: your need statement and costing
Compliance: NAFDAC, SON or local permits where relevant

blocks.title: Protect your documents
blocks.text: Your pack contains identity and bank details. Keep the folder private, use a phone screen lock, and only upload documents to official portals or send them to verified officers. Never post them in group chats. Cover or crop your BVN and account numbers when a document is only needed to show something else.

blocks.title: Planning back from the deadline
items: Day 1: confirm fit
Day 3: request statements, referees
Day 10: first draft
Day 14: checks and reader
Day 18: submit early
blocks.caption: Working backwards from the deadline leaves room for slow banks, slow referees and slow internet.

blocks.title: Worked example: Amina plans backwards
blocks.context: For example, Amina makes shea butter cream in Kano. On 1 March she finds a grant programme closing on 21 March that offers equipment to women-led cosmetics businesses.
steps: Day 1 (1 March): she confirms eligibility. Kano is included, she has a CAC business name, and the programme asks for at least one year of trading. She has two years.
She lists eight requirements in her tracker, including two references and six months of bank statements.
Day 2: she messages two referees (a shop owner who stocks her cream and her cooperative secretary) asking for a short letter by 10 March.
Day 3: she requests statements from her bank, which can take a few days.
Days 4 to 12: she drafts answers in short sessions after work, using her need statement.
Days 13 to 16: checks, and her cooperative secretary reads the whole application.
Day 18 (18 March): she submits, saves the confirmation email and screenshot, and diaries 25 April to follow up.
blocks.result: Amina submits three days early with every document attached. If the portal is slow on the final day, as portals often are, it does not affect her.

takeaways: Treat every application as a six-stage process: fit, requirements, evidence, draft, check, submit.
One tracker shows every opportunity and its next action.
A named, private document pack saves days on every application.
Plan backwards from the deadline and submit at least two days early.

activity.title: Set up your tracker and document pack
steps: Create a tracker (Google Sheet or notebook page) with the seven columns from this lesson.
Add your three shortlisted opportunities from Module 1 and fill in the stage and next action for each.
Create a private Funding Pack folder and add at least four documents, named clearly.
For your nearest deadline, write a backwards timeline with at least five dated steps.
activity.evidence: A screenshot of your tracker and of your named Funding Pack folder, plus your written timeline.

lessons.title: Checking every figure: consistency, honesty and compliance before you submit
objectives: Cross-check figures between your application, records and bank statements
Explain a difference between numbers honestly instead of hiding it
Check an application point by point against the funder's requirements
Recognise commitments in loan and grant terms before you sign

blocks.text: Every serious reviewer does the same thing first: compare. They compare the sales figure in your application with the money flowing through your bank statement. They compare the cost of the machine with the quotation you attached. They compare the number of customers you claim with the evidence you provide. When the numbers disagree and you have not explained why, trust drops sharply, and many applications are rejected at this point without the business ever being properly considered.

blocks.name: document-analysis
blocks.alt: A person examining a document with a magnifying glass
blocks.caption: Reviewers compare your figures against each other; check them yourself first.

blocks.text: The three-way check

Before submitting, put three sources side by side: **what you wrote**, **your records**, and **your bank statements**. For each key figure, they should tell the same story, or you should be able to explain the difference in one honest sentence.

head: Figure
Where it appears
What to check
rows: Statement inflows should be close to recorded sales, unless you note a share of cash sales
Same amount everywhere; quotation dated within the last few weeks
A business name registered last year can still have traded longer, but say so
Count part-time and family helpers honestly and label them
Declare every current loan; hidden loans usually show up in a credit check

blocks.title: Worked example: Chioma's sales do not match
blocks.context: For example, Chioma sells fabrics in Onitsha. Her application says average monthly sales are about ₦1,800,000. Her six months of business statements show total inflows of ₦7,200,000.
steps: Statement average: ₦7,200,000 ÷ 6 = ₦1,200,000 a month.
Gap: ₦1,800,000 minus ₦1,200,000 = ₦600,000 a month, a third of her claim.
She checks her records: about ₦500,000 a month is paid in cash and goes to an ajo contribution and stock purchases before reaching the bank.
The remaining ₦100,000 gap is because one month's figure in her draft was a festive peak, not an average.
She corrects her average to ₦1,700,000, based on her records, and adds a note: about ₦500,000 a month is cash, shown in her sales book, attached.
blocks.result: Chioma's claim is now backed by evidence and the difference is explained. A reviewer can see she is careful and honest, which is exactly what a lender is judging. She also starts banking all cash sales so the next statement tells the full story on its own.

blocks.title: Never inflate or invent
blocks.text: Adding figures, inventing customers, using someone else's photos, or editing a bank statement is dishonest, and changing a financial document can amount to forgery. It also usually fails: banks verify statements directly, credit bureaus reveal existing loans, and programmes visit winners. A smaller, true application beats a bigger false one every time.

Do the same with your **costs**. If you say the machine costs ₦650,000, attach a dated quotation for ₦650,000 from a real supplier, with their business name and phone number. If prices are rising quickly, say how old the quotation is and add a small, clearly labelled allowance for price change rather than quietly rounding up.
Point-by-point compliance

Read the call or loan form again and turn every requirement into a line on a checklist. Then tick each one only when you can point to the page or file that meets it. Watch especially for: word limits, required file types (PDF only?), the exact name format (as on your CAC certificate), signatures, dates on quotations, and questions with two parts where people answer only one.

blocks.title: Before you press submit
items: Figures match across all sources
Differences explained in writing
Every requirement ticked
Names match CAC exactly
Trusted person has read it
blocks.caption: Five checks that catch most avoidable rejections.

blocks.text: Read what you are agreeing to
Grant agreements and loan offers contain commitments that last long after the money arrives. Before you sign, find and write down each of these in plain words:

items: **Loans:** total amount repayable, every fee (management, insurance, processing), repayment dates, penalty for late payment, what happens to collateral or guarantors if you default, whether you can repay early without a charge.

**Grants:** what the money may and may not be spent on, reporting dates and format, whether you must keep receipts for a certain period, whether unspent money must be returned, use of your name and photos in their publicity.
**Both:** who to contact with problems, and what counts as breaking the agreement.

blocks.title: Ask questions in writing
blocks.text: If something in the terms is unclear, ask the officer by email or WhatsApp and keep the reply. A written answer protects you later if there is a disagreement, and a funder who refuses to explain their own terms is giving you useful information.

takeaways: Reviewers compare figures; do the three-way check (application, records, statements) first.
Explain any honest difference in one clear sentence and attach evidence.
Never inflate, invent or edit documents: it is dishonest and usually discovered.
Turn every requirement into a checklist line and tick it only with evidence.
Write down every commitment in the terms before you sign.

activity.title: Run a three-way check on your numbers
steps: Write your average monthly sales from your records for the last six months.
Add up your business bank statement inflows for the same months and divide by six.
Calculate the difference and write one honest sentence explaining it, or correct your figure.
Do the same for one other figure (item cost, staff numbers or existing loans).
List every requirement from one shortlisted opportunity and tick those you can already evidence.
activity.evidence: Your three-way check sheet showing both averages, the difference and your explanation, plus the ticked requirements list.

lessons.title: Loan arithmetic: true cost, repayment capacity and the bad-month test
objectives: Calculate the total cost of a loan, including interest and fees
Compare a flat-rate quote with a reducing-balance quote
Work out how much monthly repayment your cash flow can safely carry
Test a loan against a slow month before you sign

blocks.text: A loan is only good if your business can repay it on time **from its normal cash flow**, without borrowing again, selling assets or taking money meant for the family. This lesson gives you the arithmetic to check that yourself, instead of trusting the person selling the loan.

blocks.name: calculator
blocks.alt: A woman working with a large calculator
blocks.caption: Do the loan arithmetic yourself before anyone asks you to sign.

blocks.text: Step 1: the total cost

Ask every lender for the **full repayment schedule in writing**: each payment date, each amount, and every fee. Then add it up. Total cost = everything you will pay back minus the amount you actually receive. If a fee is taken from the loan before you receive it, you receive less money but still repay the full amount, which makes the loan more expensive than it looks.
Step 2: flat rate or reducing balance?

Many small business loans in Nigeria are quoted as a **monthly rate**. There are two very different ways to charge it. With a **flat rate**, interest is calculated on the full original amount for every month, even though you are repaying part of it each month. With a **reducing balance**, interest each month is calculated only on what you still owe. The same "3% a month" costs much more on a flat basis.

blocks.title: Same 3% a month, two methods
items: Flat rate
Reducing balance
blocks.caption: On ₦500,000 over six months, flat costs ₦90,000 in interest while reducing balance costs about ₦53,800.
right: Interest only on what is still owed

blocks.title: Worked example: two quotes for ₦500,000
blocks.context: For example, Grace sells frozen fish and chicken in Ibadan and wants ₦500,000 for six months to buy a second chest freezer and stock. Two lenders quote 3% a month.
steps: Lender A, flat: interest = ₦500,000 x 3% x 6 = ₦90,000. Total repaid ₦590,000, or about ₦98,333 a month.
Lender B, reducing balance: the equal monthly payment works out to about ₦92,300 (a loan calculator app or spreadsheet gives this). Total repaid about ₦553,800, so interest is about ₦53,800.
Month 1 at Lender B: interest = ₦500,000 x 3% = ₦15,000, so about ₦77,300 of her ₦92,300 reduces the debt. By month 6, interest is only about ₦2,700.
Lender A also deducts a 2% management fee upfront: ₦10,000. She receives ₦490,000 but repays ₦590,000, a true cost of ₦100,000.
Lender B charges a 1% fee (₦5,000), so its true cost is about ₦58,800.
blocks.result: Both lenders said "3% a month", but Lender A costs Grace about ₦41,200 more. She chooses Lender B, and only after checking Step 3 below.

blocks.title: Let a spreadsheet do it
blocks.text: In Google Sheets, the formula =PMT(3%, 6, -500000) returns the equal monthly payment for a reducing-balance loan of ₦500,000 at 3% a month over six months (about ₦92,299). Change the numbers to test any quote in seconds.
Step 3: can your cash flow carry it?

Take the last six months from your records and bank statements. For each month, work out your **free cash**: money in, minus all business costs, minus what you take home for the family. That is the money genuinely available to repay a loan. A useful measure lenders use is the **debt service coverage ratio**: free cash divided by the loan repayment. Below 1 means you cannot pay from normal cash flow. Many careful lenders look for well above 1, so that one weak month does not cause a default. A cautious personal rule is to keep the repayment at no more than about two thirds of your average free cash.
Step 4: the bad-month test

Look at your worst month in the last year and ask: if that month came again, could I still repay? Grace's slowest month leaves her ₦7,300 short. She has three choices: hold back a **repayment reserve** of one month's payment from the loan or her savings before she starts; ask for a longer term so each payment is smaller; or borrow less. She also adds the extra profit the freezer will bring (she estimates about ₦40,000 a month from selling more stock without spoilage) but she does not count that money until it actually appears in her records.

blocks.title: Collateral, guarantors and your credit record
blocks.text: If you pledge equipment, land documents or a guarantor, you are risking those if you default. A guarantor can be asked to repay for you, which can damage a friendship or family. Late payments are also reported to credit bureaus and can block future loans. Only sign when the bad-month test passes.

takeaways: Always get the full repayment schedule and add up every payment and fee.
A flat monthly rate costs far more than the same rate on a reducing balance.
Free cash = money in minus business costs minus family drawings; the repayment must fit inside it with room to spare.
Test the loan against your worst recent month and plan a reserve before signing.

activity.title: Test a real or sample loan
steps: Take one loan offer from your shortlist, or use ₦300,000 at 4% a month for six months as a sample.
Calculate the flat-rate total cost and the reducing-balance payment (use =PMT in Google Sheets).
Add every fee and work out the true cost.
Work out your free cash for each of the last six months from your records.
Run the bad-month test and write your decision: accept, ask for a longer term, borrow less, or decline.
activity.evidence: A one-page loan check showing total cost, monthly payment, six months of free cash and your written decision.

quiz.q: A lender quotes ₦400,000 at 5% a month flat for four months. How much interest will you pay?
quiz.explain: Flat interest is on the full amount every month: ₦400,000 x 5% x 4 = ₦80,000.

quiz.q: A ₦500,000 loan has a ₦15,000 fee deducted before payout. You repay ₦590,000. What is the true cost?
quiz.explain: You receive ₦485,000 and repay ₦590,000, so the true cost is ₦105,000.

quiz.q: Kemi's average free cash is ₦120,000 a month but her worst month was ₦50,000. A loan needs ₦70,000 a month. What should she do?
options: Sign, because the average covers it
Plan a reserve, seek a longer term or borrow less, because the bad-month test fails
Hide the bad month from the lender
Take a second loan to pay the first in a bad month
quiz.explain: The repayment fits the average but not her worst month. She needs a reserve, a smaller payment or a smaller loan.

quiz.q: Chioma's application says ₦1,800,000 monthly sales, but statements average ₦1,200,000. What is the best response?
options: Leave it; reviewers rarely check
Edit the statement to match
Correct the figure from her records and explain the cash portion with evidence
Remove the statements from the application
quiz.explain: Honest correction with evidence keeps trust. Editing a statement is dishonest and can amount to forgery.

quiz.q: A grant call closes on the 30th. When should Amina plan to submit?
options: On the 30th, in the evening
At least two days before the deadline
After the deadline with an apology
Only when the funder reminds her
quiz.explain: Submitting early protects against slow portals, slow internet and last-minute problems.

quiz.q: Which of these should be in a reusable Funding Pack folder?
options: Your ATM PIN and OTPs
Clear, named scans of CAC certificate, ID, statements and quotations
Screenshots of every WhatsApp group you belong to
Only photos of your products
quiz.explain: The pack holds clear, named documents funders ask for. PINs and OTPs must never be stored or shared.

modules.title: Partnerships, Using Funds Well and Your Next Round
modules.overview: Use partnerships to get resources without debt, manage and report funded money so you are trusted again, and assemble everything into your Funding Readiness Pack and 90-day plan.

lessons.title: Partnerships without debt: supplier credit, buyer deposits and written agreements
objectives: Identify partnership deals that provide resources or market access instead of cash
Calculate the cash gap created by selling on credit terms to a bigger buyer
Prepare a partnership proposal that shows what the other side gains
List what a simple written agreement or MoU must include

blocks.text: A partnership is any arrangement where another business or organisation gives you something you need, and you give them something they value in return. Done well, it can do what a loan does without interest or collateral. Done badly, it can tie you to a buyer who pays late, or a partner who takes more than they give. The difference is in the numbers and in the written agreement.

blocks.name: handshake-deal
blocks.alt: Two business people shaking hands over a deal
blocks.caption: Good partnerships are built on clear value for both sides and written terms.

blocks.text: Common partnership deals for small producers

head: Deal
What you get
What they get
Main risk
rows: Raw materials now, pay in 14 to 60 days
Missing payment dates loses the credit and the relationship
Guaranteed supply at an agreed price and quality
Penalties or refunds if you deliver late or below standard
Credit terms that delay your cash, and returns of unsold stock
Use of a machine, kitchen or licensed space
Rent, a fee or a share of output
Unclear hours, maintenance and responsibility for damage
One member failing to pay their share

blocks.text: The cash gap in a retail deal

Getting your product into a supermarket or a chain of shops feels like a win, and it can be. But big buyers often pay 30, 45 or 60 days after delivery, sometimes only for what has sold. During that time you have already paid for materials, packaging and transport. That waiting period is the **cash gap**, and you must fund it from somewhere.

blocks.title: Worked example: Ada's supermarket offer
blocks.context: For example, Ada makes chin-chin in Port Harcourt and sells about 400 packs a month at ₦1,500 each (approximate) through her WhatsApp customers. A local supermarket chain offers to stock her in three branches: 600 packs a month at a wholesale price of ₦1,200, paid 30 days after the end of each delivery month.
steps: Her cost per pack (flour, sugar, oil, eggs, packaging, gas) is about ₦750.
Supermarket profit per pack: ₦1,200 minus ₦750 = ₦450. On 600 packs: ₦270,000 a month.
Cash she must spend each month to produce 600 packs: 600 x ₦750 = ₦450,000.
Payment arrives about 30 days after the end of the month, so she funds roughly two months of production before the first payment: about ₦900,000.
She has ₦300,000 saved. Gap: about ₦600,000.

She asks her flour and oil supplier for 30-day credit (they agree, covering about ₦250,000), and asks the supermarket to start with two branches (400 packs, ₦300,000 a month, about ₦600,000 for two months).
blocks.result: With supplier credit and a smaller start, Ada's cash need falls to about ₦350,000, close to her savings. She keeps her WhatsApp customers, proves reliable delivery for three months, then grows to the third branch. She solved most of the problem with partnerships, not a loan.

blocks.text: Proposing a partnership

Partners agree when they see clear value for themselves. Before you approach anyone, write down their likely interests: a supplier wants volume and reliable payment; a retailer wants products that sell, arrive on time, and carry proper labels and NAFDAC numbers where required; an NGO wants reach into a community it serves. Then make a short proposal: who you are, what you propose, what they gain, what you need from them, and the proof that you deliver.

blocks.title: Building a partnership
items: List their interests
Show what they gain
Agree terms together
Write it down, sign
Review after three months
blocks.caption: A partnership is a negotiated deal, not a favour, and it needs a review date.

blocks.text: Put it in writing

A **memorandum of understanding (MoU)** or simple agreement does not need a lawyer for small deals, though a lawyer is wise for anything involving large sums, property or shares in your business. It should cover, in plain words:

items: The names of both parties, exactly as registered.
What each side will provide, in quantities, standards and dates.
Prices, payment terms and what happens if payment is late.
Who owns what: equipment, brand names, recipes, customer lists.
How long the agreement lasts, how to end it, and the notice period.
How disagreements will be handled, and signatures and dates of both sides.

blocks.title: Protect your recipe and your brand
blocks.text: Do not hand over your recipe, supplier list or customer list to a partner unless the agreement clearly says what they may do with it. Be very careful with anyone who asks for a share of your business in return for help: that is a permanent change of ownership, and it needs proper legal advice and registration with CAC.

takeaways: Supplier credit, buyer deposits, distribution and shared equipment can replace a loan.
Selling to big buyers on credit creates a cash gap you must calculate and fund.
Propose partnerships around the other side's interests, with proof that you deliver.
Write every partnership down: who provides what, payment terms, ownership, duration and exit.

activity.title: Design one partnership deal
steps: Choose one partner who could supply your need instead of cash (a supplier, buyer, retailer, group or organisation).
Write their three most likely interests.
If it involves credit terms, calculate your cash gap in naira.
Draft a five-line proposal message: who you are, what you propose, what they gain, what you need, proof you deliver.
List the six headings of the agreement you would want signed.
activity.evidence: Your proposal message, cash gap calculation and agreement headings, saved as a note or photo.

lessons.title: Using funds well: spending plans, funder reports and new staff
objectives: Set up a spending plan and a separate record for funded money
Track budget against actual spending and explain differences
Write a short, honest progress report to a funder or lender
Plan training and onboarding when funding brings new staff

blocks.text: Getting the money is half the job. How you use it decides whether you will ever be funded again. Funders and lenders talk to each other, and programmes often ask applicants about past grants and loans. A well-used, well-reported first grant or loan is the strongest evidence you can bring to the next one.

blocks.name: investor-update
blocks.alt: A person sending a report with charts to an investor
blocks.caption: A short, honest update to your funder builds the track record that unlocks the next round.

blocks.text: Ring-fence the money

Keep funded money separate from day-to-day takings. The cleanest way is a separate business sub-account or a second business account used only for the grant or loan. Pay suppliers directly from it by transfer, so each payment shows on the statement. Collect a receipt or invoice for every payment, photograph it the same day, and store it in a folder named after the grant or loan.

head: For every payment, keep
Why
rows: Supplier invoice or quotation with date and business name
Shows the price was agreed before payment
Transfer receipt or bank statement line
Proves the money left the funded account and to whom
Delivery note or photo of the item in place
Proves you actually received what you paid for
One line in your tracker linking all three
Lets you, or a funder's auditor, find everything in minutes

blocks.text: If you must pay a small market trader in cash, ask for a handwritten receipt with the date, item, amount, their name and phone number, and photograph the item. Keep cash payments rare, because they are the hardest to prove later.
Budget against actual
Write your spending plan from your application as a table, then add a column for what you actually spent and a column for the difference. Update it every week while you are spending.

blocks.title: Worked example: Bukola's equipment grant
blocks.context: For example, Bukola runs a small catering business in Ilorin and receives a ₦1,000,000 grant for a commercial gas cooker, a chest freezer and food hygiene training for herself and two helpers.
steps: Planned: cooker ₦450,000, freezer ₦380,000, training ₦120,000, delivery and installation ₦50,000. Total ₦1,000,000.
Actual: cooker ₦470,000 (price rose between quote and purchase), freezer ₦365,000, training ₦120,000, delivery ₦45,000.
Differences: cooker +₦20,000, freezer −₦15,000, delivery −₦5,000. The savings covered the cooker increase exactly.
She checks her grant agreement: moving money between lines is allowed up to 10% of a line without permission. ₦20,000 is about 4% of the cooker line, so she simply explains it in her report.
blocks.result: Bukola's report shows every naira, with receipts, and a one-line explanation of the price change. Had the change been larger than her agreement allowed, she would have written to the funder for approval before buying.

blocks.title: The funded money cycle
items: Plan each spend
Pay by transfer
Keep every receipt
Compare plan and actual
Report honestly
blocks.caption: Repeat this cycle every week while money is being spent, and every month while results are being measured.

blocks.text: Writing a progress report

Use the funder's format if they provide one. If not, keep it to one or two pages with these parts: what you planned, what you did, what it cost against budget, the results so far in numbers, problems and how you handled them, and what comes next. Include photos of the equipment in use or the training taking place. Report bad news early and plainly: a funder who hears about a delay from you, with a plan to fix it, reacts very differently from one who discovers it.

items: Results in numbers: "Weekly output rose from 60 to 110 meals in month two" beats "business has improved".
Compare with your starting point (the baseline) from your application.
For a loan, the lender mainly wants on-time payments; a short update when you take a big new order can still build trust for a larger second loan.

blocks.text: When funding brings new staff

Growth funding often means more hands. Plan it like any hire: write what the person will do each day, agree pay, hours and a trial period in writing, and train them before they work alone. Funded growth that outruns your ability to train people leads to poor quality, waste and unhappy customers, which then shows up in your report.

items: Write a one-page task sheet for the role, with your quality standards.
Show, then watch, then let them do it with you checking, then let them do it alone.
Train on safety first: gas, knives, hot oil, electricity and hygiene in a food business; machine guards in a workshop.
Check their work daily for the first two weeks, then weekly.

blocks.title: Safe workplace, safe report
blocks.text: If funded equipment involves gas, electricity or heat, have it installed by a qualified person, keep a fire extinguisher where staff can reach it, and show every worker how to switch off the gas and power. An accident hurts people first, and it also ends funding relationships.

takeaways: Keep funded money in a separate account and pay by transfer with receipts.
Track budget against actual weekly and explain every difference.
Report results in numbers against your starting point, and report problems early.
Train new staff with a task sheet and close checking, safety first.

activity.title: Build your funded-money tracker
steps: Take the costed need from Module 1 and write it as a budget table with lines.
Add columns for actual spending and difference.
Fill in sample actual figures (or real ones if you have funding) and calculate differences.
Write a half-page sample progress report with at least two results in numbers.
If your plan involves new staff, write a one-page task sheet for the role.
activity.evidence: Your budget-versus-actual table and sample progress report, saved or photographed.

lessons.title: Assembling your Funding Readiness Pack and 90-day plan
objectives: Assemble a complete Funding Readiness Pack from the work in this course
Check the pack against a final gap list
Write a 90-day plan that names a real opportunity and dated actions
Plan how one successful funding round leads to the next

blocks.text: This lesson brings everything together into one pack you can use for any grant, loan or partnership, and a 90-day plan to pursue a named opportunity. Funders and partners respond to preparation. Arriving with this pack ready puts you ahead of most applicants.

blocks.name: business-plan
blocks.alt: A woman presenting a business plan on a board
blocks.caption: Your pack and plan are the proof that you are ready to be trusted with growth money.

blocks.text: What goes in the pack

head: Section
Contents
Built in
rows: ID, BVN confirmation, CAC certificate, TIN, permits
Six to twelve months of business statements, monthly profit and loss, sales and expense records
Photos, customer letters, repeat orders, references, any past funding used and reported
Costed need statement, chosen route, expected results in numbers
Total cost, payment, free cash, bad-month test
Proposal message, cash gap, agreement headings

blocks.text: Keep the pack in two forms: your private digital Funding Pack folder, and a printed, labelled file for meetings with bank officers or partners. Update the financial section every month. A pack that was ready six months ago but has old statements is no longer ready.
A one-page funding proposal

Many conversations start with a single page, so write one. It should state who you are and how long you have traded; your current monthly sales and profit (from records); the exact need and its cost; how it will be funded (amount from you, from the funder or lender, from a partner); the result in numbers and by when; and, for a loan, how repayments will be met, showing your free cash.

blocks.title: Worked example: Ruth's final gap check and 90-day plan
blocks.context: For example, Ruth runs a small fruit juice and zobo business in Jos. She started this course with a readiness score of 6 out of 12. Her need: a commercial juice extractor and a chest freezer, about ₦850,000 (approximate) together, to supply two hotels that have asked for daily deliveries.
steps: Gap check now: CAC done, business account opened four months ago, records complete for six months, loan check done. New score: 10 out of 12.
Remaining gaps: only four months of business statements (her shortlisted lender asks for six), and her zobo label has no NAFDAC number, which the hotels' purchasing officer has asked about.
Funding mix: ₦200,000 of her own savings, a written 50% deposit from one hotel on its first monthly order (about ₦150,000), and a microfinance bank loan of ₦500,000.

Loan check: at the quoted 2% a month on a reducing balance over 12 months, =PMT(2%, 12, -500000) gives about ₦47,280 a month. Her worst recent month had ₦60,000 free cash; average is ₦110,000. The bad-month test passes.
Days 1 to 30: start the NAFDAC process for zobo (it takes time, so she begins at once), get the hotel deposit agreement in writing.
Days 31 to 60: sixth month of statements arrives; submit the loan application with the full pack.
Days 61 to 90: buy equipment, train her helper, begin hotel deliveries, send each hotel a monthly delivery summary.
blocks.result: Ruth's plan names a real lender, a real partner and dated actions. She knows exactly which two gaps stand between her and funding, and how long each will take.

blocks.title: Your 90-day funding plan
items: Days 1 to 30: close gaps
Days 31 to 60: apply
Days 61 to 90: use and report
Day 90: review, next round
blocks.caption: Each 90 days should end with a review and the next opportunity chosen.

blocks.text: Before you call the pack finished, hand it to one trusted person who knows business, such as a cooperative secretary, an accountant friend or a mentor, and ask them to read it as if they were the lender. Their questions show you exactly where a real reviewer would hesitate. Fix those points, then date the pack so you know when it next needs updating.
From one round to the next

Each successful round builds the next. A small loan repaid on time strengthens your credit record for a larger one. A grant used well and reported honestly becomes evidence for the next programme. A partner who has seen three months of reliable delivery is more likely to extend credit or a bigger order. Keep a short **funding history** page in your pack: what you received, from whom, for what, and the result.

blocks.title: Say no when it is right
blocks.text: Part of being funding-ready is declining offers that do not fit: a loan that fails the bad-month test, a grant whose rules would pull you away from your business, or a partner whose terms would take your brand. Every no that protects your business is a good decision.

takeaways: Your Funding Readiness Pack has seven sections; keep it digital and printed, and update records monthly.
A one-page proposal states the need, the funding mix, the result and how repayment will be met.
A 90-day plan names a real opportunity and dated actions to close the last gaps.
Each well-used round of funding is evidence for the next; keep a funding history.

activity.title: Assemble your Funding Readiness Pack
steps: Gather the outputs from every lesson into one folder in the seven sections listed.
Re-score your readiness out of 12 and list any remaining gaps.
Write your one-page funding proposal.
Write a 90-day plan naming one real opportunity, with at least six dated actions.
Ask one trusted person to review the pack and note their questions.
activity.evidence: Your completed pack folder (screenshot of contents), the one-page proposal and the 90-day plan.

quiz.q: Ada will supply a supermarket 400 packs a month at a cost of ₦750 each, paid 30 days after month end. Roughly how much cash must she fund before the first payment arrives?
quiz.explain: She funds about two months of production: 2 x 400 x ₦750 = ₦600,000.

quiz.q: Which item is most important to include in a partnership agreement?
options: Each partner's favourite colour
Who provides what, prices and payment terms, ownership, duration and how to exit
Only the partners' phone numbers
A promise to be friends
quiz.explain: These are the terms that prevent disputes about delivery, money, ownership and ending the deal.

quiz.q: Bukola's grant cooker cost ₦20,000 more than planned. Her agreement allows up to 10% movement between lines. The cooker line was ₦450,000. What should she do?
options: Hide the difference
Explain it in her report, since 4% is within the allowed movement
Return the whole grant
Stop the project
quiz.explain: ₦20,000 is about 4% of ₦450,000, within the 10% allowed. She explains it with receipts.

quiz.q: Which progress report line is strongest?
options: The business is doing very well
We are grateful for the support
Weekly output rose from 60 to 110 meals in month two
Things will improve soon
quiz.explain: Results stated in numbers against a starting point are what funders need.

quiz.q: A retailer offers to stock Tolu's product but asks for her full recipe and supplier list with no written agreement. What should she do?
options: Hand them over to build trust
Refuse to deal with retailers at all
Agree terms in writing first, and keep recipe and supplier details protected unless the agreement covers them
Ask for payment in cash only
quiz.explain: Recipes and supplier lists are valuable assets. Without written terms she could lose them.

quiz.q: Ruth's 90-day plan starts the NAFDAC process in the first 30 days. Why?
options: Because it is cheapest at the start of the month
Because regulatory processes take time and a buyer has already asked about it
Because loans require NAFDAC for every product
It does not matter when she starts
quiz.explain: Slow, necessary steps go first so they do not delay the opportunity.

finalQuiz.q: Which need is the best fit for a grant rather than a loan?
options: Stock for a confirmed supermarket order
Free hygiene training for ten young women in your community
A second freezer that raises weekly sales
Fabric for a paid school uniform order
finalQuiz.explain: Training with community value does not repay itself directly, so a grant fits; the others earn money that can repay a loan.

finalQuiz.q: On the six-area readiness check, which gap should usually be closed first?
options: Nicer product photos
Anything that makes you ineligible, such as missing registration the programme requires
A longer business story
A new logo
finalQuiz.explain: Eligibility gaps come first, then evidence gaps, then nice-to-haves.

finalQuiz.q: How should you check that a microfinance bank is genuine?
options: Trust any bank that sends you a WhatsApp message
Check that it appears on the Central Bank of Nigeria's list of licensed institutions
Ask the loan officer if it is licensed
Check how many followers it has on Instagram
finalQuiz.explain: Banks and microfinance banks are licensed by the CBN, which publishes lists of licensed institutions.

finalQuiz.q: Someone offers Halima a grant if she sends her BVN and the OTP that arrives on her phone. What should she do?
options: Send them quickly before the offer closes
Send only the BVN
Refuse, never share an OTP or PIN, and report the message
Ask for a smaller grant
finalQuiz.explain: OTPs and PINs give access to your accounts. No genuine programme asks for them.

finalQuiz.q: A loan of ₦300,000 at 4% a month flat for six months costs how much in interest?
finalQuiz.explain: ₦300,000 x 4% x 6 = ₦72,000 on a flat basis.

finalQuiz.q: Why does a reducing-balance loan at 3% a month cost less than a flat loan at 3% a month?
options: Because reducing-balance loans have no fees
Because interest is charged only on the amount still owed, which falls each month
Because the rate is secretly lower
It does not; they always cost the same
finalQuiz.explain: As you repay, the balance falls, so each month's interest is smaller on a reducing balance.

finalQuiz.q: Tunde's free cash averages ₦90,000 a month with a worst month of ₦70,000. A loan needs ₦45,000 a month. What does the bad-month test show?
options: It fails
It passes, with ₦25,000 to spare in the worst month
It cannot be calculated
It passes only in festive months
finalQuiz.explain: ₦70,000 minus ₦45,000 leaves ₦25,000 even in the worst month, and the payment is half the average.

finalQuiz.q: Your application says ₦900,000 monthly sales but statements average ₦600,000. What is the right response?
options: Increase the statement figures
Correct or explain the difference honestly with evidence such as a cash sales book
Remove the sales figure
Submit and hope no one notices
finalQuiz.explain: Reviewers compare figures. Honest correction or explanation with evidence protects trust.

finalQuiz.q: What is the main reason to submit an application at least two days early?
options: Funders always choose the first application
To avoid failure from slow portals, poor network or last-minute problems
Early applications skip the review
It is a legal requirement
finalQuiz.explain: Last-day portal and network problems are common; submitting early removes that risk.

finalQuiz.q: A retailer will pay Joy 45 days after month end. What must she calculate before agreeing?
options: Only her selling price
The cash gap: how much production she must fund before payment arrives
Her staff's birthdays
The retailer's profit
finalQuiz.explain: Credit terms delay cash. She must know how much she needs to fund in the meantime.

finalQuiz.q: Which is the best way to manage grant money once received?
options: Mix it with daily sales for flexibility
Keep it in a separate account, pay suppliers by transfer, and keep every receipt
Withdraw it all in cash
Lend some to friends until you need it
finalQuiz.explain: Ring-fencing and receipts make spending traceable and reporting easy.

finalQuiz.q: Ruth's readiness score rose to 10 out of 12, but she has only four of the six months of statements her lender requires. What does a good 90-day plan do?
options: Applies now and hopes
Schedules the application after the sixth statement arrives, and uses the wait to close other gaps
Gives up on that lender
Asks the bank to backdate statements
finalQuiz.explain: A good plan sequences actions around real requirements and uses waiting time productively.

capstone.title: Funding Readiness Pack
capstone.brief: Produce a complete Funding Readiness Pack for one real business need: organised registration documents and financial records, a numbers-based one-page funding proposal, a loan check or partnership plan as relevant, and a 90-day plan naming the opportunity you will pursue and the gaps you will close.
steps: Write your costed need statement and choose the funding route, with reasons.
Collect and name your documents and six or more months of records and statements in a private Funding Pack folder.
Run the three-way check on your key figures and correct or explain any differences.
If borrowing, complete the loan check with true cost, payment, free cash and the bad-month test; if partnering, complete the cash gap and agreement headings.
Write a one-page funding proposal and a use-of-funds budget table.
Write a 90-day plan naming one verified opportunity with at least six dated actions, and ask a trusted person to review the pack.
evidence: Readiness score out of 12, before and after
Loan check or partnership cash gap calculation
One-page funding proposal and budget table
Dated 90-day plan with the named opportunity
